results.title: A Survey of Threats Against Voice Authentication and Anti-Spoofing Systems
results.content: This survey presents a comprehensive review of the modern threat landscape targeting Voice Authentication Systems (VAS) and Anti-Spoofing Countermeasures (CMs), including data poisoning, adversarial, deepfake, and adversarial spoofing attacks. The first documented attack on a voice authentication system was recorded in the 1990s when researchers discovered that replaying a pre-recorded voice sample could effectively bypass early speaker verification systems [9]. Section 5 delves into adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted audio inputs are designed to mislead voice authentication systems during inference. After designing anti-spoofing models to prevent deepfake audio attacks, attackers have adapted by launching adversarial spoofing attacks against both the VAS and the CMs. These attacks typically involve adding subtle perturbations to AI-generated audio, crafted by speech synthesis models, to fool the authentication system and spoofing detectors. Deepfake voice attacks exploit generative models to synthesize speech that mimics a target speaker, aiming to deceive VAS. These attacks can follow a white-box paradigm, where the adversary has access to gradients of both the speaker recognition model and the spoof detector , allowing for coordinated optimization across both targets. Table 2: Summary of Data Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks on Voice Authentication Systems. Adversarial attacks introduce subtle, often imperceptible, perturbations into speech signals to mislead Speaker Recognition Systems (SRS). Deepfake speech attacks exploit advanced voice synthesis techniques, such as Voice Conversion (VC) and Text-to-Speech (TTS), to impersonate users in Speaker Recognition Systems (SRS). These attacks can bypass both automated authentication systems and human listeners by generating speech that closely mimics a target speaker’s voice, often using minimal training data.
